months.title: System Design Basics + Real RAG (Flagship Project #1)
months.focus: This is the month your AI story gets genuinely strong. You already know exactly what Physynex's retrieval system needs to do — you specified it — but it was AI-assisted, not hand-built. Now you build the same thing yourself, with real infrastructure this time.

tasks.text: Trees (~10 problems)
System design: scalability, caching, load balancing, CAP theorem (concepts only)
Embeddings deep-dive: how they're generated, what "similarity" means, chunking strategies
Trees cont. (~8 problems)
Practice designing: URL shortener, rate limiter (write it out, don't just read about it)
Vector databases: start with Chroma (fastest path to a working prototype)
Tries + Heap (~10 problems)
Practice designing: a basic chat app backend
LangChain fundamentals — retrieval chains, document loaders
Heap cont. + review (~5 problems)
Build: rebuild Physynex's retrieval pipeline yourself, from scratch, with a real vector database — same requirements, your own code this time

months.projectText: This is a genuine from-scratch build, not a refactor. You already know the spec cold (you directed it) — now you implement every piece yourself for the first time: chunking, embedding calls, similarity search, guardrail logic, red-flag detection. Don't build it inside Physynex's private codebase. Build it as a separate, standalone, public repo — a small reusable RAG engine (chunking + embedding + Chroma/pgvector retrieval) — then wire it into Physynex once it works. Two wins at once: the hands-on RAG skill you're actually missing, and a genuinely public, well-documented repo with real production usage behind it, which solves a gap you have on GitHub right now (more in Part 6).

milestones.text: ~35 more DSA problems (cumulative ~110–115)
Can whiteboard 3 classic system designs out loud, unscripted
A working, public RAG repo you wrote yourself, with a real vector database, integrated into a live product
Can defend every implementation choice — chunking strategy, embedding trade-offs, guardrail logic — because you wrote it this time, not just explain what it's supposed to do

months.raw:
### MONTH 4 — AI Agents + Advanced Full-Stack (Flagship Project #2)

**Focus:** Move from "retrieves information" to "takes action." This is the differentiator that shows up explicitly in senior AI job postings (tool use, agentic libraries, MCP) — you're building the junior version of that now.

| Week | DSA | Full-Stack | AI |
|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | Graphs — BFS/DFS (~8 problems) | WebSockets basics (real-time feature on an existing project) | Function/tool calling with LLM APIs — the core primitive under every agent framework |
| 14 | Graphs cont. (~8 problems) | Basic observability — structured logging + error tracking (Sentry or similar) on a deployed project | LangGraph basics — state, cycles, multi-step reasoning |
| 15 | Advanced Graphs (~8 problems) | — | Model Context Protocol (MCP) — read the spec, understand why it exists, build one trivial MCP tool |
| 16 | Greedy (~8 problems) | — | Build: an agentic feature with real tool-calling |

**Project — Flagship #2:** Give your AI assistant the ability to *act*, not just answer. Two options — pick based on comfort experimenting on a live product:
- **Extend Physynex:** connect the assistant to your real booking system (check availability, book a slot) via tool calling — powerful because it's a real production feature with real constraints.
- **Standalone agent project:** if you'd rather not touch Physynex's production path yet, build a fresh agentic project in the same domain (a booking/scheduling agent, or a research/support agent) as its own public repo. Lower risk, same learning, still portfolio-worthy.

Either way: this is where MCP awareness pays off directly, since it's explicitly listed as a requirement in current senior full-stack-AI postings.

**Month 4 Milestone:**
- [ ] ~32 more DSA problems (cumulative ~142–147)
- [ ] A working feature where the LLM calls a real function/tool and acts on the result (not just generates text)
- [ ] Can explain the difference between a RAG pipeline and an agent in interview-level terms
- [ ] Basic logging/error tracking live on at least one deployed project

resources.title: Primary path
resources.description: takeuforward.org/strivers-a2z-dsa-course — the site, not the YouTube channel browsed on its own. Striver (Raj Vikramaditya, ex-Google/Amazon/Media.net) has said directly not to just watch his channel top-to-bottom — the site organizes ~455 problems across ~19 topics with the right video embedded at the right point, theory and problems together, in the order you should learn them. priorityOrder.tier: Tier 1 — Never skip, even if reduced in volume
items: DSA consistency (fewer problems/week is fine; stopping entirely is not)
Testing (Jest/RTL) — cheap to learn, commonly screened for

Python fundamentals + one working RAG project (your minimum viable AI story)
System design (keep the vocabulary and 3–4 practiced designs even if you cut practice volume)
Docker (can go conceptual-only if truly squeezed)
ML fundamentals coursework (shrink to "can explain the workflow," skip the polished project)

priorityOrder.tier: Tier 3 — First things to cut if the calendar demands it
items: AI agents / MCP depth (a strong differentiator, not a baseline requirement)
Fine-tuning experiments (conceptual understanding is enough regardless)

sections.contentMarkdown:
## Part 1 — Where You Stand Today

### 1.1 Strengths & Transferable Skills

These are real, and you should stop underselling them:

- **Production React/Next.js/TypeScript depth.** 65+ shipped components, Redux/Context refactors with a measured 30%+ maintainability gain, multiple *live* products (not tutorial projects). This is your floor, not your ceiling — it's already competitive.
- **Backend-adjacent range most "frontend" candidates don't have.** Node.js middleware design, the BFF pattern, secure API proxying (sanitization, token forwarding, header injection), Express. You already think about backend concerns — you just haven't formalized the database/testing/infra side yet.
- **Genuine product-level understanding of applied AI — still rare, even without the hands-on code yet.** You specified and directed exactly what a serious AI feature needs: retrieval logic (keyword + embeddings hybrid), topic/guardrail controls, red-flag symptom detection, lead classification. Most engineers never get this far — they either avoid AI features entirely or bolt on a raw API call with no product thinking. To be precise about where you actually stand (per your own correction): the Physynex implementation was AI-assisted, so the hands-on technical depth — writing the retrieval code yourself, defending every choice under questioning — isn't there yet. That's exactly what Months 3–4 rebuild, using Physynex's own requirements as the spec. Pulled from live job postings while researching this: an Accenture "AI/ML Engineer" listing (7.5 yrs min) and a remote "Senior Full Stack AI Engineer" role (₹22–30 LPA) both ask for this shape of work. You already understand the shape of the job — the roadmap builds the hands to match.
- **Full delivery-lifecycle exposure.** CI/CD (Jenkins), deployment, third-party integrations (HubSpot, Webflow, ZeroBounce).
- **Entrepreneurial/product range that's unusual at 2–3 years in.** Physynex and Croire Paints (croirepaints.com — a live 3D product showcase using Three.js/React Three Fiber, currently not on your resume) are real, live, customer-facing products you built and shipped, not internal-only assignments. This is strong behavioral-interview material.
- **You quantify everything.** 30%+, 25%, 20%, 15% — this is genuinely good resume practice and most candidates don't do it.

### 1.2 Gap Analysis — Full Stack Developer Track

Checked against your resume, your actual GitHub, and real "Full Stack Developer" postings on Indeed India (2–6 yrs band) as of July 2026:

| Gap | Why it matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **SQL / relational databases** | Near-universal expectation alongside or instead of MongoDB. A live GLOINNT "Full Stack Developer (MERN/MEAN)" posting and a Carlton IT listing both explicitly wanted relational DB comfort, not just Mongo. | 0 mentions on resume |
| **Automated testing** | "Write clean, maintainable code and perform unit testing" appears directly in a real job description you're a strong fit for otherwise. | 0 mentions on resume/GitHub |
| **DSA / coding-interview fluency** | Still gates most Indian tech interviews regardless of role or seniority. | No LeetCode/competitive profile referenced |
| **System design fundamentals** | Standard from mid-level up; increasingly asked even at 2–3 YOE for product companies. | Not mentioned |
| **Docker** | Table-stakes for "owns a feature end-to-end" positioning. | Not mentioned |
| **One cloud platform (recommend AWS)** | Two of three detailed job postings pulled during research explicitly required AWS or Azure service familiarity, not just Jenkins CI/CD. | Not mentioned |

### 1.3 Gap Analysis — AI Engineering Track

| Gap | Why it matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **Python** | The single biggest blocker. Every AI-adjacent posting pulled — Accenture's AI/ML Engineer role, the Gen AI Solutions Engineer role, the remote Full Stack AI Engineer role — lists Python as a must-have, often "advanced." Your resume has zero Python. | 0 mentions |
| **ML fundamentals (workflow-level)** | Not deep math — but you should be able to explain train/test splits, overfitting, evaluation metrics, and when classical ML beats an LLM call. | Not present |
| **Hands-on RAG implementation** | You directed and understand the concept (retrieval, guardrails, red-flagging, lead classification) — genuinely good product instinct — but the code itself was AI-assisted. Writing and defending the implementation yourself is the real gap, not just adding a vector database on top of something you already built by hand. Treat Month 3 as building the thing for the first time, not upgrading it. | Physynex's pipeline exists and works, but wasn't hand-built by you |
| **Agent frameworks + tool use** | Every mid-to-senior AI job posting checked (Accenture, CloudiQS) explicitly asks for agentic libraries — LangChain/LangGraph, AutoGen, or AWS's Strands/Bedrock AgentCore. | Not present |
| **Model Context Protocol (MCP) awareness** | As of mid-2026, MCP has become the standard tool-interoperability layer across essentially every major agent framework (LangGraph, CrewAI, Claude Agent SDK, OpenAI Agents SDK, Strands) — and it's explicitly listed as a "must-have" in the CloudiQS senior posting. Worth knowing conceptually even before you're using it daily. | Not present |

### 1.4 Skill Tiers

**Essential (blocks you from being competitive without it):**
SQL/Postgres · Testing (Jest + RTL) · DSA · System design basics · Docker · One cloud platform · Python · Applied ML fundamentals · Real RAG with a vector database · Basic agent/tool-use pattern

**Recommended (strong differentiator, not a hard blocker):**
GitHub Actions CI/CD · Redis · WebSockets · Basic observability (error tracking/logging) · FastAPI (Python backend — several AI-engineer postings specifically want this alongside or instead of Node) · LangChain/LangGraph fluency · MCP hands-on · LLM evaluation basics · Fine-tuning concepts (conceptual, not hands-on)

**Optional (nice to have, don't chase these first):**
GraphQL · Kubernetes · React Native · Multi-cloud · Computer vision · Deep learning math / training models from scratch · Open-source contributions to third-party projects

### 1.5 Interview-Ready vs. Needs Significant Work

**Interview-ready right now:**
- React/JS/TS fundamentals, hooks, component architecture, state management patterns
- Node.js/Express, REST API design, middleware/auth/session concepts
- Explaining Physynex's AI assistant at the *product/architecture* level — what it does, why each piece exists (guardrails, red-flagging, lead classification) — you already have a 30-question prep document from an earlier session covering this and general React/JS/Node fundamentals; reuse and extend it, don't rebuild it
- Agile process questions, ownership/initiative stories (Physynex, Croire Paints)

**Needs significant work:**
- DSA in *timed coding-interview format* specifically (you code well on the job — that's a different skill from solving an unseen problem in 30 minutes)
- System design in whiteboard/verbal-reasoning format
- SQL (currently ~zero)
- Testing (currently ~zero)
- **Defending Physynex's RAG implementation at the code level** — right now, "walk me through how you built the retrieval logic" is a genuine risk area, because you can explain the *what* and *why* but not yet every implementation choice. This closes specifically in Month 3, once you've rebuilt it yourself.
- Python/ML/AI technical depth beyond the prompt-engineering level — you can't yet defend vector DB trade-offs, chunking strategy choices, or agent architecture decisions in an interview
- Cloud/deployment architecture depth (Jenkins CI/CD is real experience, but it's not the same as being able to reason about AWS service choices)

### 1.6 The Strategic Call: AI Engineer, Not ML Engineer

This distinction matters enough to state plainly, because it determines what you spend your limited hours on.

**ML Engineer / LLM Engineer** — trains, fine-tunes, and optimizes models from the inside. Requires real depth in linear algebra, probability/statistics, and frameworks like PyTorch/TensorFlow. Realistic timeline to competitive: 12–24+ months of focused study, often alongside formal coursework. Not what you're asking for, and not necessary for the roles your profile fits.

**AI Engineer** — takes existing foundation models (GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama) via API and builds reliable, production-grade *systems* around them: RAG pipelines, agents, tool-calling workflows, evaluation harnesses. Requires strong software engineering (you have this), Python, and applied understanding of LLM behavior — not model internals. This is a software engineering job with an AI-shaped surface area, and it's the fastest, highest-upside move for someone already building production software, which is exactly your position.

Market data backs this, and not just from one source: current industry comparisons describe the field shifting hard toward AI engineer roles for working software engineers specifically *because* you keep everything you already know and layer applied-AI skills on top, rather than starting a new specialization from zero. Broader India-specific data points the same direction — a July 2026 hiring report tracking 18,400+ Indian tech listings found AI Engineer roles growing faster month-over-month than any other tracked role (+21%), averaging ₹18.8 LPA, with Bengaluru alone accounting for over a third of listings; separately, "AI-Integrated Full-Stack Developer" is now named explicitly as one of the highest-demand full-stack role categories in India for 2026, which is precisely the hybrid position this roadmap is built to get you into. That's this roadmap's entire bet. Every AI-track item below (Python, RAG, vector DBs, agents, MCP) is chosen because it serves the AI Engineer path — not the ML research path.

---

sections.title: Part 2 — Reality Check
sections.contentMarkdown:
## Part 2 — Reality Check

### 2.1 What 6 Months Can Realistically Buy You

Being direct, as you asked:

- **Full Stack readiness: very achievable, close to done.** You're not starting from zero — you're closing five well-defined gaps (SQL, testing, DSA, system design, Docker/cloud) on top of a genuinely strong existing base. Six months at a sustainable pace comfortably gets you interview-ready across the mid-level Full Stack market.
- **"AI Engineer" (applied/product AI, RAG + agents): achievable and realistic.** This is a software-engineering skill layered on top of skills you already have. Six months is enough to build 2–3 genuinely strong, defensible AI-integrated projects and speak fluently about the concepts.
- **"ML Engineer" (training/fine-tuning models from scratch, research-depth math): not realistic in 6 months alongside a full-time job**, and — per the strategic call above — not the path that matches either your background or where the market is pulling. If a role explicitly demands this, it's outside this roadmap's scope; that's a 12–24 month investment with a different daily structure (much more math, much less shipping).
- **DSA depth vs. breadth.** ~180–200 problems over 6 months (detailed in Part 4) is a strong bar for mid-tier-and-above product companies and matches what most working engineers achieve in this timeframe. If you specifically target FAANG-tier companies, expect their bar to sit higher (often 300–400+ problems, refined over a longer window) — worth knowing now rather than discovering it in month 5.
- **Doing both tracks at once means slower depth in each** than focusing on one alone. The sequencing below is deliberately designed so Full Stack fundamentals (which you're closer to finishing) land first, and AI depth builds on top — so if time gets tight anywhere, you fall back to "strong Full Stack engineer with real applied-AI experience," which is itself a highly competitive, hard-to-fake position, not a failure state.

### 2.2 Your Weekly Time Budget

Built around 10 AM–7 PM weekdays (sometimes 8 PM), with burnout avoidance as a hard constraint — and restructured around single-subject focus per session, not split hours. That's the right call for technical material: switching subjects mid-session costs you the ramp-up time twice, and real understanding needs enough unbroken time to read/watch *and* immediately practice, not just skim two things shallowly.

| Day | Window | Focus (one subject, full session) | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mon | 8:30–10:30 PM | DSA — full session | 2h |
| Tue | 8:30–10:30 PM | Full-Stack topic — full session | 2h |
| Wed | 8:30–10:30 PM | DSA — full session | 2h |
| Thu | 8:30–10:30 PM | AI/Python topic — full session | 2h |
| Fri | Flexible | Light DSA review, or fully off | 0–1h |
| Sat | Morning + afternoon | Project work — one continuous focus (the mid-session break is for rest, not for switching subjects) | 4h |
| Sun | Morning | One single-focus block, rotating weekly: DSA weak-spot review, OR extended theory/course video, OR extra project time — whichever the week needs most | 2.5h |
| Sun | End of session | Logistics only — plan next week. Not a learning task, so it doesn't break the single-focus rule | 0.5h |
| Sun | Afternoon/evening | Rest — protected, not optional | 0h |

**Total: ~15–16 hrs/week → ~65–70 hrs/month → ~400–420 hrs over 6 months.** Same total as the original design — this repackages the hours into deeper, uninterrupted blocks, it doesn't add hours.

**How this maps onto the month-by-month tables in Part 3:** the "DSA" column = your Monday + Wednesday sessions. The "Full-Stack" column = your Tuesday session. The "AI/Python" column = your Thursday session. Project work = mostly Saturday, with Sunday as overflow if something needs more room that week.

**On 8 PM days:** don't try to force the full 2h block in — shift to 9:00–10:30 PM (1.5h) and keep it single-subject, just shorter. A shorter uninterrupted block beats a full-length one chopped into two subjects.

**Non-negotiable:** at least one full day off per week (built in above as Sunday evening + flexible Friday). If you miss a day, don't double up the next day to "catch up" — just resume the plan. Catch-up cramming is the single most common cause of burnout-driven quitting in self-study plans like this one.

### 2.3 Trade-offs, Stated Plainly

1. **Depth vs. breadth in DSA:** you're optimizing for "strong at most companies," not "strongest possible at any company." If a specific FAANG-tier interview appears on your calendar, you'll want a 3–4 week intensive bump beyond this plan.
2. **AI Engineer vs. ML Engineer:** covered in 1.6 — this roadmap deliberately does not chase deep ML math or from-scratch model training. That's the right call for your timeline and background, but it does mean roles that specifically want research-level ML depth stay out of reach after 6 months.
3. **Two tracks, one calendar:** if a month runs short, Part 9 tells you exactly what to cut and what to protect. Full Stack fundamentals are protected first; the more exploratory AI-agent work is the first to compress.
4. **Simultaneous job interviewing:** Months 5–6 assume you're also actively interviewing, which eats into study time. That's intentional — the point of the roadmap is to get hired, not to keep studying indefinitely.

---

## Part 6 — GitHub & Resume

### 6.1 What your GitHub actually shows right now

Checked directly (github.com/prasanthkrjha): 5 public repos — `BlogPage`, `Student-Enrollment-System`, `Weather-Update`, `dashboard-react`, `LandingPage`. These read as early-coursework projects. None of your real, production-grade work (Sangeetha Connect, Physynex, Croire Paints) has a public repo — understandably, since two are proprietary/client work. But the practical effect is that anyone who clicks through from your resume to your GitHub right now sees a much weaker signal than your actual level.

**This is exactly what Months 3–5's flagship projects are designed to fix** — they're deliberately built as new, standalone, public repos rather than changes buried inside private codebases.

**Concrete actions:**
- [ ] Add `github.com/prasanthkrjha` to your resume header — it's linked from your portfolio site but currently missing from the resume itself, which is the document ATS systems and recruiters scan first.
- [ ] Add a profile README (a repo named exactly `prasanthkrjha/prasanthkrjha`) — short intro, current focus (Full Stack + Applied AI), pinned project links.
- [ ] Once Months 3–5 projects are live, pin them (RAG engine, agentic feature, capstone) so they're what a visitor sees first — you don't need to delete the older repos, just stop leading with them.
- [ ] Each new repo: proper README (problem, architecture, tech stack, live link, screenshots, setup steps), meaningful commit history — not `fix`, `fix2`, `final fix`.
- [ ] Optional, lower priority: one or two small open-source contributions (docs fixes, small bug fixes) to a library you're already using (LangChain, a UI library) — real but not essential signal.

### 6.2 Resume Adjustments

Your resume is already in solid shape — quantified bullets, clean ATS-friendly structure, no fluff. Specific additions as your skills land, not all at once:

- **Immediately:** add the GitHub link (above).
- **After Month 3:** once the RAG engine repo is live, it's your strongest possible bullet — a standalone, open-source RAG module with a real integration, distinct from "used the OpenAI API."
- **After Month 4:** add a distinct "AI/ML Engineering" skills subsection (separate from your current "AI & Integrations" line) once Python, vector DBs, and agent frameworks are genuinely in daily use — this is what lets ATS keyword scans and recruiters searching for "AI Engineer" actually surface you.
- **Once testing is real (Month 1+):** a short line reflecting test coverage practice, either in a project bullet or the skills section.
- **Worth considering, space permitting:** Croire Paints (croirepaints.com) isn't on your resume at all right now, and it shows Three.js/3D work — a different axis than your other two listed projects. Only add it if you have room without crowding the AI story, which should stay the lead differentiator.
- **Keep the one-page discipline** you already have — resist the urge to add everything at once as new skills land.

---

## Part 7 — Interview Preparation

### 7.1 Technical Topics to Cover

**Full-stack conceptual (you're closer here than you think — extend, don't restart):**
React internals (reconciliation, rendering behavior, hooks rules, closures) · Node.js event loop · REST API design principles · database indexing & normalization · caching strategies (client, CDN, server, DB-level) · auth patterns (JWT vs. sessions) · CORS. You already have a 30-question interview-prep document from an earlier session covering React/JS fundamentals, the Node.js middleware/BFF pattern, and Gen AI/Physynex architecture at the conceptual level — treat that as your base layer for process and concept questions. Its Physynex answers cover the *what and why*; pair them with Month 3's rebuild so you can also answer the *how*, line by line, when someone digs in.

**AI/LLM conceptual (new ground — this is where you need the most reps):**
How RAG actually works end-to-end · chunking strategy trade-offs · when vector search beats keyword search (and when it doesn't) · embedding model selection trade-offs · hallucination mitigation approaches · prompt injection awareness (genuinely relevant to you — you already specified red-flag/guardrail detection for Physynex, so frame this as an extension of the security thinking you already demonstrated at the product level, now backed by Month 3's hands-on rebuild) · agent architecture patterns (the ReAct loop, tool calling, single-agent vs. multi-agent) · fine-tuning vs. RAG vs. prompting trade-offs.

**DSA & System Design:** covered in Parts 3 and 4.

### 7.2 Behavioral Preparation

Use the STAR method, and build your story bank from bullets you already have real evidence for:
- The Redux/Context refactor (30%+ maintainability) → *technical decision-making, code quality ownership*
- HubSpot/Webflow/ZeroBounce integration (25% efficiency) → *cross-functional collaboration, ambiguity*
- The Physynex retrieval pipeline (the original spec and direction) → *initiative, product thinking, translating a real user need (patient safety, lead quality) into AI feature requirements*
- The Month 3 rebuild and Month 4 agent-building work from this roadmap → *self-directed technical learning, closing your own gaps deliberately, growth mindset*
- Physynex and Croire Paints as products, not just codebases → *ownership, end-to-end thinking, entrepreneurial range*

### 7.3 Mock Interviews & Coding Practice Cadence

- **Months 1–4:** untimed DSA practice, focus on pattern recognition.
- **Month 5:** first mock interviews — Pramp (free, peer-matched) or Interviewing.io (free tier) for technical rounds; record yourself for behavioral answers and review the playback.
- **Month 6:** 1 mock interview per week minimum (technical, system design, or behavioral, rotating), plus timed LeetCode practice under interview conditions.
- Claude itself is a free, always-available option for drilling behavioral answers or talking through a system design out loud — useful between scheduled mocks, not a replacement for them.

---

sections.title: How to Use This Document
sections.contentMarkdown:
## How to Use This Document

- Each **Module** is a subject area. Each **Unit** inside it is one sitting's worth of learning — small enough to search for and finish, specific enough that the search actually returns the right thing.
- Every unit lists: the **exact concepts** inside it, the **primary resource** (verified, not guessed), a **secondary resource** if the first doesn't click, and what **"done" looks like** (problems solved / thing built / question you can now answer).
- **Tier** marks priority: 🔴 Essential (never skip) · 🟡 Recommended (strong differentiator) · 🟢 Optional (nice to have). Matches Part 9 of the roadmap — if time gets tight, drop 🟢 first, then 🟡, never 🔴.
- Sequencing matters — modules are numbered in the order that makes each one easiest to learn (e.g., SQL before RAG, Python before ML, RAG before Agents). Follow the order within a module; you can interleave modules the way the roadmap's calendar does.
- If a unit's resource isn't working for you, don't force it — the "if this doesn't land" search term is there specifically so you can find a second teacher without losing the thread.

---

# SQL Fundamentals

SQL is one of the most universally required skills across full-stack engineering roles — nearly every backend system stores relational data, and almost every engineering interview that touches data access will expect you to write or reason about SQL queries. Understanding SQL deeply, not just syntactically, is what separates candidates who can debug a slow query in production from those who can only follow a tutorial schema.

The key mental shift is recognizing that SQL is declarative: you describe the data you want, not the steps to retrieve it. The database's query planner chooses how to execute your query. This means writing better SQL is partly about writing clearer intent (which the planner understands better) and partly about understanding what the planner does so you can avoid traps like accidental full-table scans.

SQL query clauses execute in a logical order that differs from their written order: `FROM` and `JOIN` first (which tables), then `WHERE` (filter individual rows), then `GROUP BY` (aggregate), then `HAVING` (filter groups), then `SELECT` (project columns), then `ORDER BY`, then `LIMIT`. This ordering explains many "why doesn't this work?" moments — you cannot use a `SELECT` alias in `WHERE` because `WHERE` runs before `SELECT` assigns those aliases.

---

## Theory & Fundamentals

### Relational Model

Relational databases store data in tables (relations) of rows (tuples) and columns (attributes). Every table has a primary key — one or more columns that uniquely identify each row. Tables relate to each other via foreign keys, which reference a primary key in another table. This relational structure is what makes JOIN possible: when you JOIN two tables on matching key values, the database assembles composite rows from both.

### Logical Query Execution Order

Written order vs. execution order is one of the most misunderstood aspects of SQL:

```
Written order:    SELECT → FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT
Execution order:  FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT
```

Consequences:
- `WHERE` cannot reference aliases defined in `SELECT` (those don't exist yet at WHERE time).
- `HAVING` can reference aggregate functions because it runs after `GROUP BY`.
- `ORDER BY` can reference `SELECT` aliases because it runs after `SELECT`.

### Aggregation

Aggregate functions collapse multiple rows into a single value. When used with `GROUP BY`, they produce one result per group rather than one result for the entire table.

Common aggregate functions: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows; `COUNT(column)` counts non-NULL values; `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN`, `MAX` work as expected. Nulls are ignored by all aggregates except `COUNT(*)`.

### Subqueries

A subquery is a complete SELECT statement nested inside another query. Subqueries can appear in three positions:
- **In WHERE** — often with `IN`, `EXISTS`, or comparison operators
- **In FROM** — treated as a derived table (must be aliased)
- **In SELECT** — scalar subqueries returning a single value per row

---

## Core Concepts / Techniques

### SELECT Syntax and Filtering

```sql
-- Basic projection and filtering
SELECT first_name, last_name, email
FROM users
WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01'
  AND status = 'active'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 25 OFFSET 0;

-- Using LIKE for pattern matching
SELECT * FROM products
WHERE name ILIKE '%coffee%';  -- ILIKE is case-insensitive in PostgreSQL

-- NULL handling — use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL, not = NULL
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE shipped_at IS NULL;
```

### JOIN Types

```sql
-- INNER JOIN: only rows with a match on both sides
SELECT u.name, o.total, o.created_at
FROM users u
INNER JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;

-- LEFT JOIN: all rows from users, order data or NULL where no match
SELECT u.name, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
GROUP BY u.id, u.name;

-- Find users with NO orders (anti-join pattern)
SELECT u.name
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;

-- FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both sides
SELECT u.name, o.total
FROM users u
FULL OUTER JOIN orders o ON u.id = o.user_id;
```

Mental model: INNER = intersection, LEFT = "keep everything from the left table," FULL OUTER = "keep everything from either table, fill gaps with NULL."

### GROUP BY and HAVING

```sql
-- HAVING filters groups after aggregation — not the same as WHERE
SELECT
  user_id,
  COUNT(*)         AS total_orders,
  SUM(total)       AS lifetime_value,
  AVG(total)       AS avg_order_value
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'          -- filters individual rows BEFORE grouping
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3                -- filters groups AFTER aggregation
   AND SUM(total) > 100
ORDER BY lifetime_value DESC;
```

### Subqueries

```sql
-- Correlated subquery: references outer query's row
SELECT name, salary
FROM employees e
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id = e.department_id  -- references outer e
);

-- EXISTS: efficient "does at least one matching row exist?"
SELECT u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.user_id = u.id
    AND o.total > 500
);

-- Subquery in FROM (derived table)
SELECT dept, avg_sal
FROM (
  SELECT department_id AS dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
  FROM employees
  GROUP BY department_id
) AS dept_averages
WHERE avg_sal > 75000;
```

---

## Code Examples

### Complete Query: Sales Report with Aggregates

```sql
-- Monthly sales summary by product category
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('month', o.created_at)       AS month,
  c.name                                   AS category,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.id)                     AS order_count,
  COUNT(DISTINCT o.user_id)                AS unique_customers,
  SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)         AS revenue,
  AVG(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price)         AS avg_order_value
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON p.id = oi.product_id
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
WHERE o.status = 'completed'
  AND o.created_at >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', o.created_at), c.name
HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) > 1000  -- only categories with meaningful revenue
ORDER BY month DESC, revenue DESC;
```

### Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

```sql
-- CTEs make complex queries readable by naming intermediate results
WITH active_customers AS (
  SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS order_count
  FROM orders
  WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '90 days'
    AND status = 'completed'
  GROUP BY user_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2
),
customer_tiers AS (
  SELECT
    u.id,
    u.name,
    u.email,
    ac.order_count,
    CASE
      WHEN ac.order_count >= 10 THEN 'platinum'
      WHEN ac.order_count >= 5  THEN 'gold'
      ELSE 'silver'
    END AS tier
  FROM users u
  JOIN active_customers ac ON ac.user_id = u.id
)
SELECT tier, COUNT(*) AS count, AVG(order_count) AS avg_orders
FROM customer_tiers
GROUP BY tier
ORDER BY avg_orders DESC;
```

### Window Functions

```sql
-- Rank products by revenue within each category
SELECT
  p.name,
  c.name AS category,
  SUM(oi.unit_price * oi.quantity) AS revenue,
  RANK() OVER (
    PARTITION BY c.id
    ORDER BY SUM(oi.unit_price * oi.quantity) DESC
  ) AS rank_in_category
FROM products p
JOIN categories c ON c.id = p.category_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name, c.id, c.name
ORDER BY category, rank_in_category;
```

---

## Best Practices

- **Use explicit column names in SELECT** rather than `SELECT *` — it makes queries self-documenting, prevents breakage when a table's schema changes, and avoids transmitting columns you don't need.
- **Prefer JOINs over correlated subqueries in WHERE** when retrieving data — the query planner can optimize JOIN strategies far better than re-executing a subquery per row.
- **Use `EXISTS` instead of `COUNT(*)` for presence checks** — `EXISTS` short-circuits as soon as it finds one matching row, while `COUNT(*)` must scan all matching rows.
- **Filter early with WHERE before aggregating** — every row eliminated by WHERE is one less row the GROUP BY and HAVING clauses must process.
- **Use CTEs for complex queries** instead of nested subqueries — they execute once, are named, and can be referenced multiple times, which improves both readability and (in some databases) performance.
- **Be explicit about NULL handling** — use `COALESCE(column, default)` to substitute NULLs in arithmetic, and `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` for comparisons; `column = NULL` always evaluates to NULL (not TRUE or FALSE).
- **Avoid functions on indexed columns in WHERE** — `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024` prevents index use; `WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'` does not.

---

## Common Interview Questions

**Q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?**
A: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping occurs. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and aggregation. You cannot use aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, etc.) in a WHERE clause — those require HAVING.

**Q: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?**
A: INNER JOIN returns only rows where a matching row exists in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table, with NULL values for columns from the right table when no match exists. Use LEFT JOIN when you need to preserve records from one table even when the other table has no matching row.

**Q: What does GROUP BY do and what is the rule about SELECT columns when using it?**
A: GROUP BY collapses rows that share the same value(s) in the grouped column(s) into a single output row. The rule: every column in SELECT must either appear in GROUP BY or be wrapped in an aggregate function. Violating this is a SQL error in strict databases.

**Q: What is a correlated subquery and when is it a performance concern?**
A: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query, so it must re-execute for every row of the outer result set. This is an O(n) penalty on top of the outer query's cost, making it slow on large datasets. It can often be rewritten as a JOIN or a non-correlated subquery with better performance.

**Q: When would you use a CTE versus a subquery?**
A: CTEs improve readability by naming intermediate result sets and allowing them to be referenced multiple times. Subqueries are fine for simple, one-time use within a single expression. Prefer CTEs when the logic is complex, when the intermediate result is reused, or when recursive queries are needed (`WITH RECURSIVE`).

**Q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column_name)?**
A: `COUNT(*)` counts all rows including those with NULL values in any column. `COUNT(column_name)` counts only rows where that specific column is not NULL. This distinction matters when counting optional/nullable fields.

**Q: What is a window function and how does it differ from GROUP BY?**
A: Window functions (using `OVER`) perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing those rows into a single output row. GROUP BY collapses rows — you get one row per group. Window functions let you compute running totals, rankings, and lag/lead values while keeping every original row in the result.

**Q: How would you find duplicate records in a table?**
A: Use GROUP BY on the columns that define uniqueness, then filter with HAVING COUNT(*) > 1: `SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;`

---

## Practice Exercises

1. **Order analysis**: Given `users`, `orders`, and `order_items` tables, write a query that returns each user's name, total number of orders, total amount spent, and average order value — but only for users who have placed at least 3 completed orders. Sort by total amount spent descending.

2. **Category leaderboard**: Write a query that returns the top 3 best-selling products (by total quantity sold) within each product category. The result should include category name, product name, and total quantity. You may use either a window function or a subquery approach.

3. **Churn detection**: Given an `orders` table with `user_id` and `created_at`, identify users who placed at least one order in 2023 but zero orders in 2024. Write this two ways: once using a NOT IN subquery and once using a LEFT JOIN anti-join pattern.

4. **Running total**: Write a query that shows each order alongside a running total of revenue for all orders placed on or before that order's date, ordered chronologically. Use a window function.

5. **Hierarchical data**: Given an `employees` table with `id`, `name`, and `manager_id` (self-referencing foreign key), write a query using a recursive CTE that returns the full reporting chain from any given employee up to the CEO (the employee whose `manager_id` is NULL).

---

## Key Takeaways

- SQL executes in logical order — FROM, JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT — not written order; this explains many "why can't I use this alias here?" errors.
- INNER JOIN returns the intersection; LEFT JOIN preserves all rows from the left table; anti-joins (LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL) find records with no match.
- WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation; only HAVING can use aggregate functions.
- Subqueries in WHERE and SELECT re-execute per row; prefer JOINs or CTEs for performance at scale.
- Window functions (RANK, ROW_NUMBER, SUM OVER, LAG) enable per-row analytics without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does.
- NULL is not a value — it represents absence of a value; use IS NULL, COALESCE, and NULLIF to handle it explicitly.
- CTEs make complex queries readable and maintainable; recursive CTEs handle hierarchical/graph traversal without application-level loops.
- Aggregate functions ignore NULLs except COUNT(*), which counts all rows regardless of NULL values in any column.

# PostgreSQL & Database Design

Knowing SQL syntax is only half the picture. Designing a schema that remains correct and performant as data grows — and as requirements change — is the other half, and it is the half that separates engineers who can build systems from those who can only follow tutorials. Database design decisions made early are expensive to change later: a missing foreign key constraint or a poorly chosen normalization level can require a painful migration once millions of rows exist.

PostgreSQL is the most full-featured open-source relational database and the dominant choice in modern full-stack projects. Beyond standard SQL, it provides rich data types (JSONB, arrays, enums, UUID), powerful indexing options (partial indexes, GIN indexes for full-text search), advanced transaction controls, and excellent performance at scale. Understanding its specific behavior — how it enforces constraints, how its planner uses indexes, what its MVCC transaction model means for concurrent access — is directly applicable on the job.

Schema design is fundamentally about making the database enforce the rules your application depends on. Every constraint you push down to the database level is a rule that cannot be violated even if application code has a bug. Every constraint you leave to application code alone is a rule that will eventually be violated.

---

## Theory & Fundamentals

### Normalization

Normalization is the process of structuring tables to eliminate redundant storage of the same fact. When a fact is stored in only one place, updating it requires touching only one row — no risk of the same fact being inconsistently updated in some places but not others.

**First Normal Form (1NF):** Each column holds a single atomic value. No comma-separated lists, no arrays of values stuffed into a text column. Violation example: storing `"tag1,tag2,tag3"` in a `tags` column — those values cannot be individually queried or indexed. Fix: a separate `post_tags` join table.

**Second Normal Form (2NF):** Every non-key column depends on the entire primary key, not just part of it. Only relevant when the primary key is composite. Violation example: a table with primary key `(order_id, product_id)` that also stores `product_name` — product name depends only on `product_id`, not on the full composite key. Fix: move product name to the products table.

**Third Normal Form (3NF):** Every non-key column depends only on the primary key, not on another non-key column (no transitive dependencies). Violation example: storing both `user_id` and `user_email` on an `orders` table — email depends on the user, not on the order. Fix: join to the users table when you need the email.

The practical rule: normalize to 3NF by default, then deliberately denormalize specific columns only after you have measured evidence of a performance problem that normalization is causing. "I might need it to be faster" is not evidence.

### MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control)

PostgreSQL uses MVCC to allow concurrent reads and writes without readers blocking writers or vice versa. Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot of the database as of its start time. Old row versions are kept alongside new ones until no running transaction can see them, then cleaned up by VACUUM. This model provides high concurrency but means you need to understand what "consistent snapshot" means for your transaction isolation level.

### Transaction Isolation Levels

PostgreSQL supports four isolation levels. The default is Read Committed: each statement in a transaction sees only committed data at the moment that statement runs (not at transaction start). Repeatable Read gives a stable snapshot for the entire transaction. Serializable provides the strongest guarantee — concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one at a time. Most application code runs at Read Committed; use Serializable for operations where phantom reads would be dangerous (e.g., double-booking prevention).

---

## Core Concepts / Techniques

### Primary Keys and Foreign Keys

```sql
-- UUID primary keys: better for distributed systems, no sequential guessing
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "pgcrypto";

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Foreign key with ON DELETE behavior
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id         UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id    UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  -- ON DELETE RESTRICT: prevent deleting user if orders exist
  -- ON DELETE CASCADE: delete orders when user is deleted
  -- ON DELETE SET NULL: set user_id to NULL when user is deleted
  status     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending'
    CHECK (status IN ('pending', 'processing', 'shipped', 'completed', 'cancelled')),
  total      NUMERIC(12, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (total >= 0),
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

### Constraints as Correctness Guarantees

```sql
-- NOT NULL: the column must always have a value
-- UNIQUE: no two rows can share this value
-- CHECK: arbitrary boolean condition must be true
-- REFERENCES: the value must exist in the referenced table

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  sku         TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  price_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents > 0),
  stock       INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock >= 0),
  category_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES categories(id)
);

-- Multi-column unique constraint (same user can't review same product twice)
CREATE TABLE reviews (
  user_id    UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id),
  product_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  rating     INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (rating BETWEEN 1 AND 5),
  body       TEXT,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, product_id)   -- composite PK also enforces uniqueness
);
```

### Indexing

```sql
-- B-tree index (default): good for equality, range queries, ORDER BY
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user_id ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_created_at ON orders(created_at DESC);

-- Compound index: efficient for queries filtering on both columns
-- Column order matters: put the most selective column first
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_status_created ON orders(status, created_at DESC);

-- Partial index: only indexes rows matching a condition
-- Much smaller than a full index if the condition filters most rows
CREATE INDEX idx_pending_orders ON orders(created_at)
WHERE status = 'pending';

-- Unique index: enforces uniqueness and also speeds lookups
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email);

-- Check which indexes exist on a table
SELECT indexname, indexdef FROM pg_indexes WHERE tablename = 'orders';

-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see if an index is being used
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 'abc-123' AND status = 'pending';
```

### Transactions

```sql
-- Multiple statements that must all succeed or all roll back
BEGIN;

-- Deduct stock
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock > 0;

-- Check the update actually happened (row might have been at 0)
-- Application code checks affected row count; if 0, ROLLBACK

-- Create the order
INSERT INTO orders (user_id, product_id, total)
VALUES ($2, $1, $3);

-- Create the order item
INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price)
VALUES (lastval(), $1, 1, $3);

COMMIT;

-- If any statement errors, or application explicitly calls:
ROLLBACK;  -- all changes are undone, as if none happened
```

### Migrations

```sql
-- Schema changes should be applied as numbered, sequential migration files
-- Never edit a migration that has already run in production

-- Migration 0003_add_user_preferences.sql
ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN preferences JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}';

-- Safe column addition: adding a nullable column or one with a default
-- is instant in PostgreSQL 11+ (default is stored in catalog, not rewritten)

-- Adding NOT NULL to an existing column: requires backfilling first
UPDATE users SET preferences = '{}' WHERE preferences IS NULL;
ALTER TABLE users ALTER COLUMN preferences SET NOT NULL;
```

---

## Code Examples

### Full Schema: E-Commerce Core

```sql
-- Clean schema with proper constraints and indexes

CREATE TABLE users (
  id         UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  email      TEXT NOT NULL,
  name       TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT users_email_unique UNIQUE (email),
  CONSTRAINT users_email_format CHECK (email LIKE '%@%')
);

CREATE TABLE categories (
  id        UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  name      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  parent_id UUID REFERENCES categories(id)  -- self-referencing for hierarchy
);

CREATE TABLE products (
  id            UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  category_id   UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES categories(id),
  name          TEXT NOT NULL,
  price_cents   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (price_cents > 0),
  stock         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (stock >= 0),
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  user_id     UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending',
  total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  CONSTRAINT orders_status_check CHECK (
    status IN ('pending','processing','shipped','completed','cancelled')
  )
);

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id),
  quantity   INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price > 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

-- Indexes for common access patterns
CREATE INDEX ON orders(user_id);
CREATE INDEX ON orders(status, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX ON order_items(product_id);
CREATE INDEX ON products(category_id);
```

### Using EXPLAIN to Diagnose Slow Queries

```sql
-- EXPLAIN shows the query plan without running the query
-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs it and shows real timings
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT u.email, COUNT(o.id) AS order_count
FROM users u
JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id
WHERE o.created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '30 days'
GROUP BY u.id, u.email
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 2;

-- Look for:
-- "Seq Scan" on a large table = likely missing index
-- High "rows" estimates that differ widely from actual = stale statistics
-- "Hash Join" vs "Nested Loop" vs "Merge Join" — planner picks based on row counts
-- Run ANALYZE tablename; to refresh statistics if estimates are way off
```

---

## Best Practices

- **Always use foreign key constraints** — they are the only reliable way to prevent orphaned records; application code alone will eventually fail to enforce referential integrity.
- **Use `TIMESTAMPTZ` (timestamp with time zone) instead of `TIMESTAMP`** — stores UTC internally, renders correctly for any time zone, and avoids entire classes of daylight-saving bugs.
- **Store money as integer cents** — floating-point types (`FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`) cannot represent all decimal values exactly and will silently accumulate rounding errors in financial calculations; `NUMERIC(12,2)` or integer cents avoids this.
- **Add `NOT NULL` to every column that always has a value** — NULL means "unknown," and columns that should always have a value being nullable causes confusion in aggregates and join logic.
- **Index foreign keys** — PostgreSQL does not automatically index foreign key columns (unlike some other databases), so a lookup of "all orders for user X" on an unindexed `user_id` is a full table scan.
- **Use `ON DELETE RESTRICT` as the safe default for foreign keys** — it prevents deletion of referenced rows, which forces you to handle cleanup explicitly rather than accidentally cascading deletes; use `CASCADE` only when child row deletion is genuinely desired.
- **Run migrations in transactions** — wrap schema changes in `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` so a failed migration is automatically rolled back rather than leaving the schema in a half-applied state.

---

## Common Interview Questions

**Q: What is the difference between a primary key and a unique constraint?**
A: Both enforce uniqueness, but a table can have only one primary key (which also implicitly adds NOT NULL) and can have many unique constraints. The primary key is the canonical identifier for a row and is what foreign keys in other tables reference.

**Q: What are the three normal forms and why do we normalize?**
A: 1NF requires atomic column values (no lists in a cell). 2NF requires every non-key column to depend on the whole primary key. 3NF requires no transitive dependencies between non-key columns. Normalization eliminates redundant storage so each fact exists in exactly one place, preventing update anomalies.

**Q: What is an index and what is the trade-off of adding one?**
A: An index is a separate data structure (typically a B-tree) that maps column values to their row locations, allowing the database to find matching rows without scanning every row in the table. Trade-off: faster reads at the cost of slower writes (every insert/update/delete must also update each index) and additional disk space.

**Q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE vs ON DELETE RESTRICT mean?**
A: ON DELETE CASCADE automatically deletes child rows when the referenced parent row is deleted. ON DELETE RESTRICT (default) prevents deletion of the parent row if any child rows reference it. CASCADE is convenient but dangerous if applied broadly; RESTRICT forces explicit handling of related data before deletion.

**Q: What is a database transaction and what does ACID mean?**
A: A transaction is a group of statements that execute as a single atomic unit. ACID: Atomicity (all succeed or all roll back), Consistency (the database moves from one valid state to another), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't see each other's intermediate state), Durability (committed transactions survive crashes).

**Q: When should you use a UUID primary key instead of a serial integer?**
A: UUIDs are better when: records are created across multiple services or databases that must merge (no collision risk), IDs must not be sequentially guessable for security, or you need to assign an ID before the row is committed. Serial integers are simpler, smaller (4 vs 16 bytes), and slightly faster for index lookups.

**Q: What is a partial index and when is it useful?**
A: A partial index only indexes rows that match a WHERE condition. It is useful when most queries target a specific subset of rows (e.g., only pending orders, only active users) — the index is smaller and faster to maintain than a full-table index.

**Q: What does EXPLAIN ANALYZE tell you and when should you use it?**
A: EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query and shows the actual query plan, estimated vs. actual row counts, and execution time at each step. Use it when a query is slow to diagnose whether it is doing a full table scan instead of using an index, or when the planner's row estimates are wildly off (suggesting stale statistics).

---

## Practice Exercises

1. **Schema design from scratch**: Design a schema for a blog platform with users, posts, comments, and tags. Define all primary keys, foreign keys, and NOT NULL constraints. Add at least two indexes based on the access patterns you would expect, and justify each one.

2. **Normalization exercise**: Given this denormalized table — `orders(order_id, user_id, user_email, user_name, product_id, product_name, product_category, quantity, unit_price)` — identify which normal form is violated and produce a fully normalized 3NF schema.

3. **Transaction safety**: Write a SQL transaction that transfers "loyalty points" from one user to another. The transfer should fail atomically if either the deduction or the credit fails, and should prevent the balance from going negative.

4. **Index diagnosis**: Given a slow query that filters `orders` by `status = 'pending'` and `created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days'`, use EXPLAIN ANALYZE output to determine whether an index is being used. Write the CREATE INDEX statement that would help this query and explain why you chose the column order.

5. **Constraint design**: Add a CHECK constraint to an `events` table to enforce that `end_time > start_time`. Then write a migration that adds a `cancelled_at` column (nullable TIMESTAMPTZ) and a partial index on `user_id` that only covers events where `cancelled_at IS NULL`.

---

## Key Takeaways

- Schema constraints (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK) are correctness guarantees enforced by the database itself — they are more reliable than application-level validation alone.
- Normalization (1NF → 3NF) ensures each fact is stored in one place, eliminating update anomalies; denormalize deliberately and measurably, never preemptively.
- Foreign keys must always be indexed in PostgreSQL — they are not indexed automatically, and unindexed FK columns cause full table scans on parent-child joins.
- Transactions group multiple statements into an atomic unit; if any statement fails or the application calls ROLLBACK, all changes in the transaction are undone.
- EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the primary tool for diagnosing slow queries — look for sequential scans on large tables as a signal that an index is missing.
- Use TIMESTAMPTZ not TIMESTAMP, and store monetary values as integer cents rather than floating-point — these two decisions prevent entire categories of subtle bugs.
- A partial index that targets only the rows most queries touch is often more efficient than a full index — smaller, faster to maintain, and just as useful for those queries.
- Schema migrations should be versioned, sequential, run inside transactions, and never edited after they have been applied to any environment.

# Docker

Docker solves the "it works on my machine" problem by packaging an application together with everything it needs to run — the runtime, dependencies, configuration, and operating system libraries — into a portable, reproducible unit called a container. This means the same container that runs correctly on your laptop runs identically in a CI pipeline, on a staging server, and in production. That guarantee is what makes Docker table-stakes for modern deployment workflows.

The fundamental distinction in Docker is between an image and a container. An image is an immutable, layered snapshot of a filesystem — your code, its runtime, and its dependencies frozen at a point in time. A container is a running instance of an image — a live process with an isolated filesystem, network, and resource view. You build images; you run containers from them. The same image can be used to start many containers simultaneously, each independent.

Understanding Docker well means understanding how the layer cache works, because that knowledge directly translates to faster build times. Docker builds images in layers, one instruction at a time. If the filesystem state for a layer has not changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached layer instead of rebuilding it. The practical implication: put instructions that change infrequently (installing OS packages, copying package.json) before instructions that change frequently (copying source code), so source code changes only invalidate the last few layers.

---

## Theory & Fundamentals

### Docker Architecture

The Docker daemon (`dockerd`) is a background service that manages images, containers, networks, and volumes. The Docker CLI (`docker`) sends commands to the daemon via a REST API. Images are stored in a registry (Docker Hub is the public default; AWS ECR, GitHub Container Registry, and self-hosted registries are common alternatives). When you run `docker pull image:tag`, the daemon downloads layers from the registry; when you run `docker push`, it uploads them.

### Image Layers

Every instruction in a Dockerfile creates a new read-only layer on top of the previous one. Layers that have not changed are cached and reused. A final union view of all layers makes up the image's filesystem. When a container starts, a thin writable layer is added on top — changes the container makes are written to this writable layer and discarded when the container stops (unless mounted on a volume).

### Networking

Docker containers run in isolated network namespaces. By default, containers can reach the internet (via network address translation through the host) but are not reachable from outside unless ports are explicitly published. Docker provides built-in DNS — in a Docker network, containers can reach each other by their service or container name, not by IP address. This is why `docker-compose.yml` services can reference each other by name.

### Volumes

Container filesystems are ephemeral — when a container stops or is removed, any data written to its filesystem is lost. Named volumes and bind mounts persist data across container restarts. A named volume is managed by Docker and stored in Docker's storage area. A bind mount maps a specific path on the host machine into the container — useful during development to get live code reloading without rebuilding the image.

---

## Core Concepts / Techniques

### Writing a Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Start from an official base image — tag explicitly to avoid surprise upgrades
FROM node:20-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy dependency manifests first — this layer changes only when
# package.json or package-lock.json changes, allowing layer caching
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
# npm ci is faster and stricter than npm install (requires package-lock.json)
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

# Copy the rest of the source code
# This layer invalidates on ANY source file change — comes after npm ci
# so dependency installation is still cached on source-only changes
COPY . .

# Build the application
RUN npm run build

# Document which port the app listens on (informational — doesn't publish it)
EXPOSE 3000

# The default command to run when a container starts from this image
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
```

### Multi-Stage Builds

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: build
FROM node:20-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

# Stage 2: production image
# Only the compiled output is copied — node_modules for dev and build tools are excluded
FROM node:20-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev   # install only production deps in the final image
COPY --from=builder /app/dist ./dist

ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
# Result: a much smaller production image — no devDependencies, no source files
```

### Essential Docker Commands

```bash
# Build an image from the Dockerfile in the current directory
docker build -t my-app:latest .
docker build -t my-app:v1.2.3 .       # with a specific tag
docker build --target builder .         # stop at a specific multi-stage stage

# Run a container
docker run -p 3000:3000 my-app:latest           # host:container port mapping
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 my-app:latest        # -d: detached (background)
docker run -e DATABASE_URL=postgres://... my-app # pass environment variables
docker run --rm my-app npm test                  # --rm: delete container after it exits

# View running containers
docker ps
docker ps -a  # all containers, including stopped ones

# View logs
docker logs <container-id>
docker logs -f <container-id>  # follow (stream) logs

# Execute a command in a running container
docker exec -it <container-id> sh  # open an interactive shell

# Stop and remove
docker stop <container-id>
docker rm <container-id>

# Image management
docker images
docker rmi my-app:latest
docker system prune  # remove all stopped containers, unused images, networks
```

---

## Code Examples

### Docker Compose for a Full-Stack App

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
version: '3.9'

services:
  app:
    build:
      context: .
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      DATABASE_URL: postgres://appuser:apppass@db:5432/appdb
      REDIS_URL: redis://cache:6379
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy   # wait for the healthcheck to pass
      cache:
        condition: service_started
    restart: unless-stopped

  db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: appuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: apppass
      POSTGRES_DB: appdb
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data    # named volume: data persists
      - ./init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql  # run on first start
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U appuser -d appdb"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

  cache:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data
    command: redis-server --appendonly yes   # enable AOF persistence

volumes:
  db-data:    # named volume: managed by Docker, persists across restarts
  redis-data:
```

### Development Compose Override

```yaml
# docker-compose.dev.yml — override for local development
# Usage: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.dev.yml up
version: '3.9'

services:
  app:
    build:
      target: builder          # use the dev/build stage instead of production
    volumes:
      - .:/app                 # bind mount: source changes reflected instantly
      - /app/node_modules      # anonymous volume: don't overwrite node_modules from host
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
    command: npm run dev       # hot-reload dev server instead of production start
```

### .dockerignore

```
# .dockerignore — same syntax as .gitignore
# Prevents these files from being sent to the Docker daemon as build context
node_modules
.git
.env
.env.local
dist
coverage
*.log
.DS_Store
README.md
```

---

## Best Practices

- **Use specific image tags** (`node:20-alpine`, not `node:latest`) — `latest` can change when a new major version is released, silently breaking your build; pin to a specific version.
- **Order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changed** — put `COPY package*.json` and `RUN npm ci` before `COPY . .` so source code changes do not invalidate the dependency installation layer.
- **Use multi-stage builds for production images** — the builder stage can include devDependencies and build tools; the final stage includes only what is needed to run the application, producing a significantly smaller and more secure image.
- **Never put secrets in a Dockerfile or commit them in a build context** — secrets in Dockerfile instructions are baked into image layers and visible in `docker history`; pass them at runtime via environment variables or Docker secrets.
- **Use a `.dockerignore` file** — prevents `node_modules`, `.git`, `.env`, and other unnecessary files from being included in the build context, which speeds up builds and avoids accidentally baking local secrets into images.
- **Use named volumes for database data** — bind mounts for databases are unreliable across platforms; named volumes managed by Docker are portable and correctly persist data across container restarts.
- **Use health checks in production Compose files** — `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy` ensures dependent services wait for a database to actually be ready to accept connections, not just for the container process to have started.

---

## Common Interview Questions

**Q: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?**
A: An image is an immutable, read-only snapshot of a filesystem containing an application and its dependencies. A container is a running instance of an image — a live, isolated process. Multiple containers can be started from the same image simultaneously, and they are independent of each other.

**Q: How does Docker's layer cache work and how does it affect Dockerfile ordering?**
A: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a cached layer. If nothing affecting a layer has changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of re-executing the instruction. This means frequently changing instructions (like copying source code) should come after infrequently changing ones (like installing dependencies) — otherwise a source code change invalidates the dependency installation cache.

**Q: What is a multi-stage build and why is it useful?**
A: Multi-stage builds use multiple `FROM` instructions in a single Dockerfile. Each stage can have a different base image. The final stage copies only the output of previous stages — for example, compiled binaries from a build stage — and excludes build tools, devDependencies, and source files. The result is a smaller, more secure production image.

**Q: What is the difference between a named volume and a bind mount?**
A: A named volume is managed by Docker and stored in Docker's internal storage area; it is portable and platform-independent, recommended for databases and persistent application data. A bind mount maps a specific host filesystem path into the container; it is tied to host path structure and commonly used in development to share source code for live reloading.

**Q: How do containers in Docker Compose communicate with each other?**
A: Docker Compose places all services in the same project on a shared Docker network. Each service is reachable by its service name as a DNS hostname. For example, an `app` service can connect to a `db` service at `db:5432` without any extra network configuration.

**Q: What happens to data written inside a container when the container stops?**
A: Data written to the container's writable layer is lost when the container is stopped and removed. To persist data beyond a container's lifetime, it must be stored in a named volume or a bind mount, which exist independently of any specific container.

**Q: What is the purpose of EXPOSE in a Dockerfile?**
A: `EXPOSE` is documentation — it indicates which port the application inside the container listens on. It does NOT publish the port to the host machine. To publish a port, you must use `-p host:container` with `docker run` or `ports` in docker-compose.yml.

---

## Practice Exercises

1. **Containerize an existing app**: Take a Node.js/Express application and write a Dockerfile for it. Use a multi-stage build: a build stage that installs all dependencies and compiles TypeScript, and a production stage that contains only the compiled JavaScript and production `node_modules`. Verify the production image runs correctly with `docker run`.

2. **Docker Compose setup**: Write a `docker-compose.yml` that runs your app alongside PostgreSQL and Redis. Configure the app to connect to both using service names as hostnames. Add a healthcheck to the database service and use `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` to prevent the app from starting before the database is ready.

3. **Development workflow**: Create a `docker-compose.dev.yml` override file that bind-mounts your source code into the container and runs the app with hot-reloading (`nodemon` or equivalent). Verify that changing a source file without rebuilding the image is reflected in the running container.

4. **Layer cache optimization**: Given a Dockerfile that copies all files first and then runs `npm install`, explain why this is suboptimal and rewrite it to maximize cache utilization. Verify your improvement by timing both build approaches after making a trivial source code change.

5. **Environment variable security**: Starting from a Dockerfile that has a hardcoded database password in an `ENV` instruction, refactor it to accept secrets only at runtime via environment variables. Write the `docker run` command that passes the secret value, and explain why baking secrets into images is a security risk (hint: `docker history`).

---

## Key Takeaways

- An image is an immutable snapshot; a container is a running instance — multiple containers can run from the same image, each isolated from the others.
- Docker builds images in layers; unchanged layers are cached — order Dockerfile instructions from least to most frequently changed to maximize cache reuse.
- Multi-stage builds produce smaller, more secure production images by excluding build tools, devDependencies, and source files from the final stage.
- Container filesystems are ephemeral — use named volumes for databases and persistent data; use bind mounts during development for live source code reloading.
- Docker Compose services communicate via DNS using their service names as hostnames; no hardcoded IPs are needed or desirable.
- Never put secrets in a Dockerfile — they are stored in image layers and visible in `docker history`; pass them at runtime via environment variables.
- `.dockerignore` reduces build context size, speeds up builds, and prevents local secrets (`.env` files) from being sent to the Docker daemon.
- Health checks with `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` ensure dependent services wait for actual readiness, not just for a container process to have started.
